headline: FEMA awards $3.67M to New Hampshire fire and EMS agencies
dek: The grants will help 27 Granite State jurisdictions buy protective gear, medical equipment, radios, training and a new tanker, according to the state’s congressional delegation.
body: Fire departments and emergency medical organizations across New Hampshire are set to receive $3,670,649.05 in federal Assistance to Firefighters Grants, funding that will pay for protective equipment, training, communications gear and emergency vehicles, according to a Sept. 25 [announcement from the state’s congressional delegation](https://www.shaheen.senate.gov/news/press/new-hampshire-congressional-delegation-celebrates-more-than-36-million-in-federal-funding-to-support-granite-state-firefighters).

The awards cover 27 jurisdictions and agencies, from the North Country to the Seacoast. The largest single grant is $500,000 for training equipment at the New Hampshire Department of Safety in Concord. Hancock is slated to receive $428,571.42 for a tanker, while Seabrook is set to get $390,946 for paramedic training. Colebrook’s 45th Parallel Emergency Medical Services is listed for $298,384.76 for CPR devices and cardiac monitors, and Keene is listed for $198,181.81 for power cots and power-lift systems.

Other awards are aimed at needs that are less visible to the public but central to safe emergency response. Goshen is slated for $180,523.80 for firefighter breathing apparatus, Hebron for $162,680.95 for the same type of equipment, and Weare for $125,047.61 for portable radios. Meredith’s $37,819.42 award is designated for wildland-firefighting personal protective equipment, while Rumney and Surry are each slated to buy equipment to wash and dry contaminated protective clothing.

The delegation’s announcement came from U.S. Sens. Jeanne Shaheen and Maggie Hassan and Reps. Chris Pappas and Maggie Goodlander. Because the release was issued by elected officials, the award totals and descriptions are attributed to that announcement. [WMUR](https://www.wmur.com/article/fema-first-responder-grants/73895544) separately reported that the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s awards were approaching $4 million statewide and highlighted training equipment for the Department of Safety, breathing devices for Littleton and wildland equipment for Meredith. [News Radio Keene](https://www.newsradiokeene.com/news/new-hampshire/keene-spofford-and-surry-secure-federal-firefighting-money/) separately reported the awards for Keene, Spofford and Surry.

The Assistance to Firefighters Grants program is administered by FEMA and is intended to improve the ability of fire departments and other eligible organizations to protect firefighters and the public. The [U.S. Fire Administration](https://www.usfa.fema.gov/a-z/grants/) says the program can support equipment, apparatus, training and other resources, including efforts that improve firefighter health and safety. That makes the New Hampshire awards more than a one-time equipment purchase: they can reduce the burden on local departments that must maintain specialized gear and medical-response capacity with limited municipal budgets.

The list also shows how uneven emergency-service needs can be across the state. Some awards target traditional fire suppression, such as turnout gear, breathing apparatus and thermal-imaging cameras. Others support the medical side of calls, including paramedic education, power cots, CPR devices and cardiac monitors. Vehicle and communications awards address the practical problem of moving personnel and equipment quickly across rural roads and between communities that rely on mutual aid.

The money will not put every project into service immediately. Local governments and agencies must accept the awards, follow federal grant requirements and complete the purchases or training described in their applications. The delegation’s published list identifies intended uses and dollar amounts; it does not establish a single statewide completion date. Residents should look to their own fire department, ambulance service or town government for updates on when equipment arrives or training begins.

For New Hampshire residents, the immediate impact will vary by community, but the intended result is statewide: better-equipped responders arriving at fires, medical calls and other emergencies. The awards also give local officials a concrete funding source at a time when departments face rising equipment prices, training demands and the continuing need to protect responders from hazards encountered on the job.
